summary: For 5–6 year olds, teach the four seasons as a repeating, observable yearly cycle anchored to first-hand sensory evidence: typical weather, clothing, and visible natural-world changes (buds and blossom in spring, long warm days in summer, falling leaves in autumn, bare trees and short cold days in winter). Introduce day length concretely through the child's own experience (dark at bedtime in winter, still light in summer) rather than any Earth–Sun mechanism. Keep it purely descriptive and pattern-based; the WHY of seasons (Earth's axial tilt) is explicitly deferred to later years. Build understanding over the real year through ongoing observation — a class weather chart, a seasons display, revisiting the same tree — paired with illustrated/sorting activities that make the cycle visible and let children actively decide 'which season?'.
misconceptions: Thinking it is hotter in summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun (cause is deferred, but the closeness idea appears even early and should not be reinforced).
Believing the seasons are the same everywhere in the world at the same time (ignoring hemispheres/climates).
Treating seasons as fixed calendar dates rather than gradual observable change.
Assuming day length is the same all year, or not connecting darker evenings with winter.
Over-generalising local weather (e.g. 'summer is always sunny', 'it always snows in winter').

activities.title: Tap-around year wheel: one season at a time
steps: Explore a four-part year wheel (spring, summer, autumn, winter) by choosing a season to look at closely.
For each season, look at an illustrated scene with spoken labels: the weather, what a child wears, the same tree changing, animal behaviour, and a simple long/short day-length bar or sun arc.
Compare summer (bright scene, child in a sun hat, leafy tree, long high sun arc) with winter (bare branches, coat and scarf, short low sun that sets early).
Follow the same tree through all four scenes and notice how the pictures loop back to the start.
Use a 'what comes next?' flap to predict the following season before revealing it.
activities.insight: Each season has its own look, weather and day length, and the four seasons repeat as a cycle — the same tree shows the change, and the year loops back to where it started.

activities.title: Spin the year and sort the clues
steps: Spin a year dial and watch a scene morph gradually from one season to the next, feeling the cycle turn.
Drag season clues — blossom, snowman, falling leaves, sun hat — onto the matching season.
Decide 'which season?' for each clue and check against spoken feedback.
activities.insight: Children actively decide which season a clue belongs to, and experience the year turning as a continuous cycle rather than fixed separate pictures.

activities.title: Ongoing real-world observation
steps: Keep a class weather chart over weeks and months, recording warm/cold, sunny/rainy/snowy.

Revisit the same real deciduous tree (one that loses its leaves) across the year and draw or photograph how it changes (blossom or new leaves, full leaves, falling leaves, bare). Evergreen trees keep their leaves all year, so they will not show this full pattern.
Notice and talk about when it is dark at bedtime and when it is still light outside, judging daylight by known times rather than by looking at the Sun.
Talk about what clothes people wear as the weather changes.
activities.insight: The seasonal cycle is something you can see happening in your own environment over the real year, grounded in lived experience.

activities.title: Short spoken check: name the season and read the clues
steps: Look at a picture (e.g. bare trees, children in hats and thick coats, going dark early in the afternoon) and say which season it is and which things in the picture show it.
Order the four seasons in their repeating cycle (say which season comes after winter).
Answer: when are the days longest and when are they shortest?
Answer a probe: if a warm sunny day happens in the middle of winter, does that make it summer? Why not?
Answer a probe: what might you see happening to trees or animals that tells you spring is coming?
activities.insight: Reading several seasonal signs together (weather, trees, daylight, clothing, animals) is more reliable than judging from a single cue, and days are longest in summer and shortest in winter.

checkQuestion: Look at this picture: bare trees, children in hats and thick coats, and it is going dark early in the afternoon. Which season is it, and what things in the picture told you? And through the year, when are the days longest and when are they shortest?
checkAnswer: Winter. Clues: bare trees, warm clothes and cold weather, and it getting dark early (short days). Days are longest in summer and shortest in winter, and the pattern repeats every year.
